title: Weckatuck (Neck and Spring)
summary: Weckatuck is a neck and spring placename near the foot of Long Beach by Noyack Road, associated with a nearby Native village and shell-heap site.
activity_update_summary: Removed a second description that repeated the same Weckatuck location text.
ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
why_this_matters: At Weeckatuck, the translation "end of the woods" or "end of the cove or creek" ties the name directly to the Noyack landscape around Mill Pond, now Trout Pond, where Shinnecock families are remembered as living into the late nineteenth century. The takeaway is that place names are not decorative labels; they can preserve geography, seasonal knowledge, and evidence of continuing Native presence that later local histories often treat as fading away.
introduction_content: Weckatuck is recorded as a neck of land and running spring near the foot of Long Beach, about three miles from Sag Harbor on the Noyack road.
oral_history_content: In 1966, Princess Nowedonah, Lois Hunter, released an oral history of Wickatuck in an album titled The Enchanted Spring, An American Indian Legend, published by Folkway Records FC 7753. Below are the tracks that describe the history of Wickatuck, Shelter Island, and parts of Montauk. youtube.com
history_content: A Native village stood a short distance from the spring, and later antiquarian work described a large shell-heap site in this Northside/Weckatuck landscape. Dated source references appear in the historic moments below.
legends_and_lore_content: Ca. 1600’s – Weckatuck Springs, once located at the corner of Noyack Rd. and Long Beach, Sag Harbor, and was a fresh water spring that emerged out of the cliffs that had healing properties. Various tribal people came there, in some cases all the way from Montauk during times of sickness to drink the natural spring water. 1
translation_content:
Recorded forms include Weckatuck, Weeckatuck, Wecatuck, and Wickatuck. Two possible readings are given: end of the woods or trees, and end of the cove or creek.

Why Place Names Matter

“Place names can describe the qualities of a location, relate to a sacred or historical narrative, denote a food source or all of the above.”

— University of Colorado Boulder Libraries, The World of Printed Maps: Indigenous place name maps (2023), map interpretation paragraph
preservation_content: Weckatuck connects spring water, shell-heap archaeology, trails, and Shinnecock presence in the Noyack and Sag Harbor landscape.
whereintheworld_title: On This Site, Off This Site
whereintheworld_content: Approximate marker near the foot of Long Beach and Noyack Road, used for Weckatuck neck-and-spring context rather than a precise spring, village, or shell-heap coordinate.
